purpose: This medicine is used to treat certain types of cancer, including breast cancer, stomach cancer, and lung cancer that have a protein called HER2 on their surface. It is typically used when other treatments have already been tried. Your doctor chose this medicine because your cancer tests showed it may respond well to it.
how_it_works: Think of this medicine as a smart missile — it has two parts working together. One part (trastuzumab) is a targeting agent that finds and locks onto cancer cells that have the HER2 protein. The other part is a powerful chemotherapy drug that gets delivered directly inside the cancer cell to destroy it, while trying to spare healthy cells as much as possible.
common_side_effects: You may feel nauseous, tired, or lose your appetite. Hair thinning or loss, vomiting, constipation, or diarrhea are also common. Your blood counts may drop, which can make you more prone to infections or feeling very fatigued. Most side effects can be managed, so tell your care team how you are feeling.
warnings: This medicine carries a serious risk of lung problems called interstitial lung disease (ILD) or pneumonitis — contact your doctor right away if you have new or worsening shortness of breath, cough, or fever. It can also harm an unborn baby, so use reliable birth control during and after treatment. It may lower your heart function over time, so your heart will be monitored regularly. Do not breastfeed while taking this medicine.
typical_dosing: This medicine is given through an IV infusion (into a vein) at a clinic or infusion center, usually once every 3 weeks. The dose is based on your body weight. Each infusion takes about 30 to 90 minutes depending on how well you tolerate it. Your doctor will decide the exact dose and schedule that is right for you.
